newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa reserves edge up, helped by bond proceeds.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa reserves edge up, helped by bond proceeds.

text.p: South Africa's official gold and foreign exchange reserves edged up in October, despite central bank sales of dollars to support the rand, figures released on Thursday showed.
The Reserve Bank said reserves rose by 241.5 million rand in October to 10.28 billion, even though foreign credit lines of 612 million were repaid in the month.
Economists said the increase -- which surprised the market which had been expecting a fall to around 9.6 billion rand -- reflected proceeds from the government's foreign bond issues.
Equisec economist Dawie Roodt said if proceeds of the $300 million Yankee bond issue were stripped out of reserves, it left the central bank with net reserves of roughly 8.8 billion rand.
This was lower than the net reserves of about 9.4 billion rand in September, excluding the foreign credit lines of 612 million rand credit which the bank drew down that month.
Reserves also got a boost from a higher rand gold price, which lifted gold's contribution to overall reserves to 60 percent of total gross reserves.
In dollar terms, reserves still dipped marginally and economists said the position remained critical, with official holdings of gold and foreign currencies representing just four weeks import cover.

At prevailing month-end exchange rates, October's reserves amounted to $2.17 billion, down from $2.22 billion in September, and the lowest level since early 1994 when confidence was hit by political fears in the run-up to elections.
By end-1995 reserves surged back to $4.4 billion as post-apartheid South Africa sucked in increasing foreign investment -- but the a run on the rand which started in February 1996 sent them tumbling.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said earlier this week that low reserves were the biggest single problem facing South Africa at present.
The authorities have come under mounting pressure to take action to abolish foreign exchange controls but Stals arues such calls are unreasonable in the face of such low reserves.

Optimists argue that remaining foreign exchange controls on residents would send a clear signal of the government's confidence in the economy which in turn would prompt foreign investors to return to the country.

But Stals and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel have to balance against this pent-up demand to take money out of the country. Some 10 billion rand of blocked funds are currently held in the country by South Africans who have emigrated and who might be expected to ship out those funds as soon as allowed.

At the same time, many residents want to diversify their investments by purchasing overseas assets -- particularly in view of the continuing pressure on the rand which last week hit an all-time low of 4.77 against the dollar.
The currency, which has been hit by speculative selling on the back of concerns about structural problems in the South African economy, has since recovered to around 4.70.
